card.name: A single‑storey, 400 cm‑high, 400 ×
card.summary: A single‑storey, 400 cm‑high, 400 × 300 cm wooden treehouse with bedroom loft, bathroom, and roof‑top skylight, anchored to four steel brackets on mature trees.
card.description: The backyard treehouse rises 400 cm above the ground, anchored to four sturdy steel brackets that hug the trunks of mature oaks. A 400 cm × 300 cm platform of treated pine decking forms the base, its joists spaced at 30 cm intervals for maximum rigidity. Cedar siding panels, 10 cm thick, wrap the perimeter, providing a warm, natural façade that echoes the colonial bungalow aesthetic while respecting the tree's silhouette. A modest gabled roof, framed with glulam trusses and clad in classic asphalt shingles, shelters a skylight that pours daylight into the loft sleeping area. The front entrance features a solid oak door on a hinge, flanked by double‑slide windows that invite breezes. A ladder climbs to the platform, and a low railing with hand‑rail ensures safety. Inside, a compact bathroom with a ceramic toilet, a built‑in cedar bench, and a ceiling light complete the functional living space. All exterior surfaces are finished in weather‑proof paint to protect against the elements, and the structure complies with local arborist recommendations, preserving the health of the supporting trees.
plan: Measure the selected mature trees, their trunk diameters and branch spacing, then sketch a site plan showing the tree locations and the intended footprint of the treehouse.

Draft a scaled design using hand‑drawn elevations and a simple CAD model that incorporates a 400 cm wide by 300 cm deep platform, 400 cm overall height, and a single‑storey layout with a sleeping loft, a small bathroom, and a covered porch.
Obtain permits and consult an arborist to confirm the load‑bearing capacity of the trees and to design adjustable steel brackets that will not damage the bark.
Order all lumber, fasteners, roofing, and hardware, then prefabricate floor joists, wall panels, and roof trusses in the workshop to exact dimensions.
Raise the platform by hoisting the pre‑assembled floor onto the tree brackets, secure the walls, install the roof, then attach the ladder, railing, door, and interior fixtures.
Finish the treehouse with weather‑proof paint, install lighting and a low‑flow toilet, then conduct a final safety inspection before handing over the keys.
assumptions: The treehouse is intended for a single family, so a single sleeping loft and one bathroom are sufficient.
A 400 cm overall height provides comfortable headroom while staying within typical tree canopy limits.
The footprint of 400 × 300 cm fits within a standard backyard and respects the 1‑storey height range of 200‑600 cm.
Materials are chosen for durability and ease of construction: treated pine for structural members, cedar for interior finishes, and galvanized steel for brackets.
questions: What is the maximum load the selected trees can safely support, and are there any preferred attachment methods to protect the bark?
Do you require any utilities (electricity, water) to be run to the treehouse, and if so, what capacity is needed?
Should the treehouse include any specific accessibility features such as a ramp or wider ladder?

gates.tape: height_cm 10 over 1 storey(s) is 10 cm per floor. height_cm is the WHOLE building, floor to roofline, and each floor must land between 200 and 600 cm. For 1 storey(s) that means roughly 200-600 cm.

card.name: A single‑story cedar treehouse with ladder
card.summary: A single‑story cedar treehouse with ladder, natural finish, and no electricity provides a safe, elevated play space in the backyard.
card.description: The backyard treehouse rises 300 cm above a sturdy oak, its 250 cm‑high platform supported by steel‑clamped cedar beams that hug the trunk without harming the bark. A 300 cm‑tall ladder of natural‑finish cedar provides a graceful ascent, while a low‑profile handrail follows the ladder’s line for safety. The floor is a seamless deck of twelve 300 cm‑long cedar boards, spaced to allow rain to pass, and framed by four 200 cm joists anchored to the support brackets. Four 250 cm cedar studs define each wall, sheathed with 200 cm×250 cm panels that retain the natural grain, painted only with a clear protective finish to showcase the wood’s warm hue. A single 80 cm×200 cm hinged door opens onto the platform, and two 60 cm sliding windows frame the surrounding garden, each glazed with tempered safety glass. The roof, a modest 150 cm‑deep pitch, is decked with cedar planks and finished with thirty overlapping asphalt shingles, shedding water efficiently. A surrounding railing of four posts and rails, topped with a low handrail, encircles the deck, and a nylon safety net drapes across the perimeter for added security. The entire structure is sealed with silicone at every joint, load‑tested, and inspected to meet residential safety standards, delivering a whimsical yet robust retreat for children and adults alike.
plan: Measure the selected mature tree circumference, branch spread, and clearance to determine platform dimensions and load capacity.
Draft a scaled 2‑D layout and a 3‑D BIM model that positions the floor, walls, roof and ladder relative to the trunk.
Procure cedar lumber, steel brackets, asphalt shingles and stainless‑steel fasteners sized to the BIM specifications.
Fabricate the floor joists, decking and support brackets off‑site, then hoist them into the canopy and bolt them to the tree with clamps.
Erect wall studs, attach sheathing panels, install the door, windows and safety railing according to the model’s LOD 300 details.
Install roof rafters, deck the roof, apply shingle underlayment and nail asphalt shingles, then affix the ladder to the exterior wall.
Apply a clear sealant, conduct a load‑test, and perform a final inspection to certify safe occupancy.
assumptions: The selected tree is a mature oak with a trunk diameter of at least 40 cm and a branch spread that accommodates a 250 cm×350 cm platform without interfering with foliage.
The tree can support a live load of 500 kg, allowing the cedar platform, occupants and stored gear to be safely distributed across the brackets and support beams.
Local building codes require a minimum 100 cm high safety railing and a perimeter safety net, which are incorporated into the design.
Because no electricity is requested, all fasteners are stainless steel to resist corrosion, and the finish is a clear, UV‑resistant sealant rather than painted surfaces.
questions: What is the maximum allowable live load for the tree according to a structural engineer’s assessment?
Do you prefer a fixed ladder or a removable ladder for seasonal storage or tree growth considerations?
Is a specific roof pitch or overhang length desired to match the aesthetic of the existing house?

card.summary: A 1‑storey, 4‑room colonial bungalow with shingle siding, white walls, and classic roof, built to 792 cm × 1417 cm footprint and 280 cm height.
card.description: The colonial bungalow rises gracefully from its 792 cm × 1417 cm lot, a single‑storey composition of shingle‑clad walls painted a crisp white that catches the morning light. Four well‑proportioned rooms and a single bath are arranged to minimise steps, with a cozy breakfast nook nestled beside a modern efficiency kitchen that boasts built‑in wooden cabinets. The roof, capped with classic asphalt shingles, slopes gently to a modest eave, echoing the modest yet dignified Dutch‑Colonial influence of the era. Exterior windows, eight in total, slide open to invite breezes, while the front and rear doors swing on sturdy hinges, framing the entryways with a welcoming sense of homeliness. Inside, hardwood flooring runs the length of the home, supporting plastered interior walls that define the living, dining, bedroom, and bath spaces. The ceiling is finished with smooth gypsum drywall, and the house is equipped with full electrical, plumbing, and HVAC systems concealed within the walls and roof cavity. A simple metal mailbox anchors the front façade, and a modest wooden telephone cabinet sits near the kitchen, completing the period‑appropriate yet functional domestic setting.
plan: Measure the lot, stake out the 792 cm × 1417 cm footprint, and create a site‑plan with grading contours.
Draft the floor plan, elevations, and structural layout for a 1‑storey colonial bungalow with 4 rooms and a bath, then review with the client.
Apply for building permits, order lumber, shingles, windows, doors, and all interior finish materials.
Excavate the site, install formwork, and pour a 20 cm thick concrete foundation slab.
Frame the floor joists, erect exterior wall studs, install roof trusses, and apply sheathing and roofing underlayment.
Install doors, windows, interior partitions, finishes, services, and conduct a final inspection before occupancy.
assumptions: The exterior wall colour is assumed to be white, a common choice for colonial bungalows.
Three bedrooms are inferred from the four‑room layout, leaving one room for living space.
No garage or porch is provided because the reference designs for the Desoto do not list these elements.
A standard roof pitch of approximately 30 degrees is assumed to accommodate the shingle roofing and dormer‑style silhouette.
questions: Do you prefer a specific exterior paint colour other than the assumed white?
Would you like to add a garage or carport to the design, and if so, what size?
Are there any additional interior features such as a sunroom, mudroom, or extra bathroom you would like incorporated?

card.summary: A 1‑storey, 3‑bedroom colonial bungalow with a front porch, workbench, and red toolbox, built to 792 × 1417 × 280 cm dimensions.
card.description: The single‑storey colonial bungalow occupies a tidy 792 cm × 1417 cm lot and rises 280 cm from slab to roof ridge. White wood‑shingle siding wraps the perimeter, while a modest front porch of concrete slab and wooden railing greets visitors. A solid front door with brass handle swings on a hinge, and six operable windows slide to admit breezes. Inside, three bedrooms, a living room, a kitchen with twelve pine cabinets, and a single bathroom are arranged for efficient circulation. A hardwood floor runs throughout, capped by gypsum ceiling tiles. A dedicated workbench alcove measures 150 × 60 × 90 cm, supporting a bright red metal toolbox (40 × 30 × 30 cm) for the homeowner's projects. The house is finished with asphalt shingles, a timber roof truss system, and all standard MEP services, delivering a functional, period‑appropriate residence ready for occupancy.

Order all structural and finish materials, then schedule trades for foundation, framing, roofing, and interior finishes.
Excavate, pour a concrete slab foundation, and install perimeter footings to support the wood‑frame walls.
Erect the wood‑frame walls, install windows, doors, roof trusses, and apply asphalt shingles to complete the envelope.
Finish interior finishes, install the workbench and red toolbox, then conduct a final inspection and obtain occupancy approval.
assumptions: Wall colour is assumed white because the brief did not specify a hue.
The garage is omitted as the reference designs did not include one and the brief gave no instruction.
Ceiling height is set at 260 cm to stay within the 200‑600 cm floor‑to‑roof range for a single storey.
The porch is defined as a small front porch of 300 × 200 cm based on typical colonial bungalow proportions.
